47664:
The first Christians already had a Bible: the Old Testament. Alongside it they treasured the words of Jesus and the teaching of the apostles (2 Thess 2:15; 1 Thess 2:13). Very early, apostolic writings began to be treated as Scripture. Second Peter places Paul's letters alongside 'the other Scriptures' (2 Pet 3:15-16). First Timothy quotes Deuteronomy and a saying found in Luke together, calling both 'Scripture' (1 Tim 5:18; Deut 25:4; Luke 10:7).

In the second century, a teacher named Marcion (around 144) rejected the Old Testament and kept only an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul. Partly in response, church leaders said more clearly which books they had received. Irenaeus (around 180) insisted there are four Gospels, no more and no fewer (*Against Heresies* 3.11.8). The Muratorian Fragment, usually dated to the late second century (some argue for the fourth), lists most of our New Testament.

Some books took longer. Eusebius (around 325) recorded that Hebrews, James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John and Revelation were still questioned in some places (*Church History* 3.25). In 367 Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, gave the first known list of exactly our 27 books. The regional councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) confirmed the same list for their churches.
47666:
The early church used several tests when weighing a book. Did it come from an apostle or someone close to one (*apostolicity*)? Did it agree with the faith handed down, sometimes called the 'rule of faith' (*orthodoxy*; see Gal 1:8-9)? Was it read widely in worship across the churches (*catholicity*, meaning 'universal')? Was it old enough to come from the apostolic age (*antiquity*)?

The councils did not vote books into holiness. They recognised which books the churches had already been reading and living by, the way a court might recognise someone as a citizen rather than make them one. Protestant scholars such as Michael Kruger stress that the books carried their own authority, which God's people heard. Catholic and Orthodox Christians agree the books were inspired before any council, but stress that the Spirit-led church needed to define the list with authority.

It is also honest to say the process was long and human. Some books were debated for centuries, the edges of the Old Testament still differ between churches, and books like the *Gospel of Thomas* were known but not widely read in worship. Many Christians see in this slow, communal process the same pattern as Lesson 1: God working through people, not around them.

47784: No originals, but a mountain of copies
47785:
None of the original documents written by Moses, Isaiah, Paul or John survives. Scholars call the originals *autographs*. What we have are *manuscripts*: copies made by hand, first on papyrus (paper made from reeds) and later on parchment (prepared animal skin). Copying by hand was slow, skilled work, and every copyist could make mistakes.

For the New Testament, over 5,800 Greek manuscripts are catalogued, from tiny scraps to complete Bibles. There are also about 10,000 Latin manuscripts, many in Syriac, Coptic and other ancient languages, and countless quotations in the writings of early Christian teachers. No other ancient book comes close to this number, and few have copies so close in time to when they were written.

For the Old Testament, the standard Hebrew text is the *Masoretic Text*, named after the Masoretes, Jewish scribes who between about AD 600 and 1000 added vowel signs and detailed notes to protect every letter. The oldest complete copy is the Leningrad Codex (1008), the basis of most modern Hebrew Bibles; the Aleppo Codex (about 930) is older but partly lost. The Greek Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls give us much older witnesses.
47787:
In 1947 Bedouin shepherds found jars of scrolls in a cave near Qumran, by the Dead Sea. Over the next decade eleven caves yielded remains of more than 900 manuscripts, copied between about 250 BC and AD 68. Around 230 of them are biblical books. Every book of the Old Testament is represented except Esther.

The most famous is the Great Isaiah Scroll, copied around 125 BC. It is about a thousand years older than the oldest complete Masoretic manuscripts, yet its text agrees closely with them, apart mostly from spelling and small differences. This showed how carefully the Hebrew text had been passed on.

The scrolls also showed that, before the first century, more than one form of some books was in circulation. A Samuel scroll (4QSam-a) often agrees with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text, and a shorter form of Jeremiah matches the Septuagint. A scroll of Deuteronomy reads 'sons of God' at Deut 32:8 where the Masoretic Text reads 'sons of Israel'. Modern translations use this evidence, and their footnotes often say so.
47789:
A *codex* is a book with pages, as opposed to a scroll. Early Christians adopted the codex very quickly, perhaps because it could hold several Gospels or letters together and was easy to carry.

The oldest New Testament pieces are papyri. P52, a fragment the size of a credit card held in Manchester, has a few lines of John 18:31-33 and 18:37-38. It is often dated to around AD 125-175, though some scholars, such as Brent Nongbri, argue that a later date is possible. P46 (around 200) contains most of Paul's letters, P66 (around 200) much of John, and P75 (around 175-225) parts of Luke and John. P75 is remarkably close to Codex Vaticanus, made more than a century later, which shows careful copying.

The great fourth- and fifth-century codices are complete or nearly complete Bibles in Greek. *Codex Vaticanus* (about 300-350) has been in the Vatican Library since at least the 1470s. (The learner's notes call it 'variantas'; the name is Vaticanus.) *Codex Sinaiticus* (about 330-360) was found by Constantin von Tischendorf at St Catherine's Monastery in Sinai in 1844 and 1859; it is the oldest complete New Testament and also contains the *Epistle of Barnabas* and the *Shepherd of Hermas*. Its leaves are now divided between London, Leipzig, Sinai and St Petersburg, and can be viewed online. *Codex Alexandrinus* (early 400s) was given to King Charles I of England in 1627 by Patriarch Cyril Lucaris and is in the British Library.
47790: What a variant is, and three famous ones
47791:
A *textual variant* is any place where manuscripts differ. Scholars estimate there are several hundred thousand variants in the New Testament manuscripts, more than the roughly 138,000 words of the Greek New Testament. That sounds alarming, but every difference in every copy is counted. The great majority are spelling, word order (which barely matters in Greek), 'Christ Jesus' versus 'Jesus Christ', or an obvious slip. A small number make a real difference to a verse, and a very few involve whole passages.

The ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) is missing in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; Vaticanus leaves a blank column after Mark 16:8, as if the scribe knew of something more. Most scholars think Mark originally ended at 16:8 or that the original ending was lost. The resurrection appearances in verses 9-20 are also told in the other Gospels, but the snake-handling and poison-drinking verses (Mark 16:17-18) occur only here.

The woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and appears in different places in later ones, sometimes after Luke 21:38. Many scholars think it is a true early story about Jesus that was added to John later. The 'Johannine Comma' in 1 John 5:7-8 ('the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one'), found in the KJV, appears in no Greek manuscript before the medieval period and entered Erasmus' Greek New Testament only in his 1522 edition. The Trinity does not depend on it: the church confessed the Trinity at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) without it, from passages such as Matt 28:19 and 2 Cor 13:14.
47793:
*Textual criticism* is the careful comparison of manuscripts to find the earliest form of the text. 'Criticism' here means judgement, not attack. Its main tools are simple to grasp. Manuscripts are weighed, not just counted. Earlier copies usually matter more. The best reading is the one that best explains how the others arose. A harder reading is often older, because scribes tended to smooth difficulties, not create them. Readings found in many regions are stronger than readings found in one.

Manuscripts fall into rough families. The *Alexandrian* (from Egypt: P75, Vaticanus, Sinaiticus) is usually the earliest and most careful. The *Western* (Codex Bezae, Old Latin) is early but freer. The *Byzantine* (most later Greek manuscripts) became the standard text of the Greek church. A *Caesarean* family is now doubted by many scholars.

Erasmus printed the first published Greek New Testament in 1516 from a handful of late Byzantine manuscripts. Its descendants, later called the *Textus Receptus* ('received text'), lay behind the KJV of 1611. Since the 1800s, older manuscripts have changed the picture. Westcott and Hort (1881) judged that only a tiny fraction of the text, around one part in a thousand, was still seriously in doubt. Today the Nestle-Aland (28th edition, 2012) and United Bible Societies editions underlie most modern translations, and newer computer-assisted methods continue the work. Scholars as different as Bruce Metzger and Bart Ehrman agree that the text can be recovered to a very high degree, while still debating how much the remaining differences matter.
